extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, perception researchers, and educated general readers interested in mental imagery and hallucination
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, characterising, and explaining different forms of visual mental phenomena (mental images, visions, hallucinations, illusions, phantasmagoria) and the physiological, hereditary, and social conditions that produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria distinguishing visions from mental images
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasts between 'visions' and 'mental images' as diagnostic features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visions differ from mental images in several specific respects: visions are 'entirely independent' of volition while images are 'entirely subservient to the will'; visions appear and vanish suddenly whereas images are formed comparatively slowly and fade slowly; visions are very vivid and like what one sees in broad daylight while images are vague and shadowy like the back of a theatre stage; visions seem close and 'fill the whole head' while images seem farther away in a 'far-off recess of the mind.' Use these criteria (voluntariness, suddenness, vividness/clarity, perceived proximity) to classify a visual phenomenon as a vision versus an image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: hallucination vs illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical definitions distinguishing hallucinations from illusions and noting a hybrid case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hallucinations are 'appearances wholly due to fancy'; illusions are 'fanciful perceptions of objects actually seen.' There is also a hybrid case where fanciful visions are fancifully perceived (an induced visual cloud or blur interpreted into a hallucination). When evaluating a reported percept, determine whether there was an external stimulus (illusion) or purely internally generated appearance (hallucination), and consider hybrid interpretations where induced imagery is misinterpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of illusion construction (the 'faces in the fire' process)
rubrics_metrics.description: How accidental sensory patterns and eye/attention dynamics lead to illusory percepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction of illusions often depends on the small instantaneous field of gaze and the wandering path of the eye, which follows a course influenced by (1) the easiest sequence of muscular motion, (2) idiosyncrasy, (3) the current mood, and (4) associations. Through an unconscious 'trial and error' the eye selects a track that strings together accidental marks into a coherent picture; incongruities are disregarded and deficiencies supplied by fantasy. Galton uses a 'diorama' analogy (three lanterns) to explain retention, discard, and supplied content. These factors explain how illusory faces/figures are built from ambiguous stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative strength of automatic visual sequences versus volition
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency of automatic chains of imagery to resist voluntary control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatism of the brain often produces a rapid series of changing images that are 'imperative in their refusal to be interfered with' by deliberate will. Attempts to force imagery into a chosen form commonly fail or produce hybrid forms until the automatic series concedes. When assessing attempts to will imagery, note the frequent struggle and limited efficacy of volition against strong automatic visual sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and contexts of phantasmagoria
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical features and situational triggers of phantasmagoria (crowds of phantoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phantasmagoria commonly appear as a crowd of phantoms hurrying past like men in a street; they are more often seen in the dark, frequently at the instant of putting out a candle, and generally when a person is in bed preparing to sleep (but not yet asleep). Many sane, well-functioning individuals report such experiences. Use these situational and phenomenological markers when categorising reports of crowd-like visual hallucinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and situational causes conducive to visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily and situational states that predispose to visions and hallucinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States such as fasting, prolonged wakefulness (sleep deprivation), solitary musing, and certain spiritual disciplines (self-mortification) are cited as conducive to visions. Temporary deprivation (e.g., being long deprived of food during an excursion) and protracted wakefulness produce episodes half-dream and half-hallucination. Conversely, social amusement is beneficial in reducing such phenomena. When evaluating incidence or eliciting visions, take account of these physiological and situational antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary and racial tendencies in visualisation and synaesthesia
rubrics_metrics.description: The inheritable component and possible racial/familial clustering of vivid visualisation and related phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peculiarities of visualisation (e.g., Number-Forms, associating colour with sound) are 'strongly hereditary,' and the tendency to be a 'seer of visions' also appears inheritable. Galton suggests such faculties may cluster in families or races (e.g., second-sight seers of Scotland, Gipsies). Consider familial history and cultural/racial background when assessing predisposition to vivid imagery or visionary experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and plurality of visual phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that visualisation, visions, and hallucinations form a continuum and can coexist in differing forms within the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a continuity from near absence of imagery to complete hallucination, but this continuity also involves changes in the character of the process so that two very different forms can be concurrent in the same person. The boundary is not purely intensity-based; qualitative differences matter. Use a spectrum/concurrent-forms model rather than a strict categorical separation when classifying visual phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of memory and composite recollection in constructing visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Visions and phantasmagoria often arise from patchworks or blends of past recollections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many visions are 'patchworks built up of bits of recollections' or blended memories analogous to composite portraiture. This blending provides a near-infinite variety of possible combinations for phantasmagoria faces. In analysis, look for identifiable elements drawn from recent perceptual experience or memory that could have been incorporated into the visionary content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cultural modulation of expression (nurture influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: How social attitudes and encouragement shape whether visionary tendencies are expressed publicly or repressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fantasies are laughed at and discouraged in childhood, the tendency to experience visions may be blunted by repression; if social opinion becomes favourable to supernaturalism, seers come forward and their faculty may be elaborated through encouragement, dwelling, and religious sanction. Thus the prevalence and outward expression of visions in a population reflect cultural tolerance and reinforcement as well as innate propensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial sensitiveness hypothesis for dreams and hallucinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed physiological account linking partial brain sensitiveness during sleep to dream characteristics and to hallucination-like states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dreamers show 'absence of common sense' because dreaming involves imperfect irrigation/blood-supply to the brain, leading to partial sensitiveness where some stages of mental processes are represented vividly while others are suppressed. This hydraulic analogy suggests that partial activation of brain domains can produce isolated vivid stages that emerge as visions or hallucinations. Consider cerebral perfusion/state as an explanatory factor in nocturnal and related phenomena.
